I understand that your builds are failing during dependency resolution despite no code changes. This is a known issue often caused by unpinned dependencies releasing new incompatible versions, runtime mismatches between the build environment and local machine, or corrupted build cache artifacts [DOC-DEPLOY-003]. To resolve this, please try the following steps:

1. Pin your dependencies with exact versions and commit the lock file, as unpinned dependencies are the most common cause [DOC-DEPLOY-003].
2. Compare the runtime version declared in your build configuration against the version you use locally [DOC-DEPLOY-003].
3. Clear the build cache from the settings page and trigger a fresh build to rule out a corrupted artifact [DOC-DEPLOY-003].
4. If a specific dependency is failing, check whether its registry is reachable from the build network [DOC-DEPLOY-003].

Additionally, build logs retain the full resolution output for thirty days, which can help identify which version changed [DOC-DEPLOY-003].

items.title: Rolling back a failed release
items.passage: # Rolling back a failed release **Applies to:** Container Service, Functions ## Symptoms - A release has introduced errors and must be reverted - The previous revision is needed while a fix is prepared ## Common causes - A defect reached production that testing did not catch - A configuration change had unintended effects ## Resolution

items.title: Rolling back a failed release
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Open the revisions page for the service and identify the last revision that was healthy. 2. Select roll back on that revision. Traffic moves within roughly thirty seconds and no rebuild takes place. 3. If the release included a database migration, roll the migration back before the service, or the older code will encounter a schema it does not expect. 4. Record the incident and the reason for the rollback before deploying a fix, while the detail is still fresh. ## Notes Rollback restores the container image and its configuration together. It does not restore data.

items.title: Build failures caused by dependency resolution
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Pin your dependencies with exact versions and commit the lock file. Unpinned dependencies are the cause in the large majority of cases of this kind. 2. Compare the runtime version declared in your build configuration against the version you use locally. 3. Clear the build cache from the settings page and trigger a fresh build to rule out a corrupted artefact. 4. If a specific dependency is failing to resolve, check whether its registry is reachable from the build network. ## Notes Build logs retain the full resolution output for thirty days, which is usually enough to identify which version changed.

items.title: Responding to a suspected account compromise

items.title: Multi-factor authentication setup and recovery
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Ask the user to check that automatic time synchronisation is enabled on the device generating the code. Drift is the most common cause by a wide margin. 2. If the device is lost, the user should sign in with one of their recovery codes and then re-enrol a new device from the security page. 3. Where no recovery codes are available, an account administrator can reset multi-factor authentication for that user from the team members page. 4. If the user is the sole administrator and has no recovery codes, identity verification through support is required and takes up to one business day. ## Notes Support cannot disable multi-factor authentication without identity verification, regardless of urgency.

result.answer:
Hi,

To prevent secrets from appearing in your logs, you should store them as secrets rather than standard environment variables. Secrets are masked in logs and are not readable through the API after creation [DOC-DEPLOY-004].

Since your secrets are currently being printed at startup, please treat them as exposed and rotate them immediately, even if your logs are private [DOC-DEPLOY-004]. To rotate them, you should first revoke the exposed credentials, then issue replacements with the narrowest scope that still works [DOC-SEC-002]. You should also search your audit logs for any use of the exposed credentials from unfamiliar addresses during the time they were visible [DOC-SEC-002].

After updating your configuration to use secrets, remember to redeploy your application, as running containers do not pick up new values without a restart [DOC-DEPLOY-004].

Best regards,
Support Team
result.answer_reason: The documentation explicitly states that secrets are masked in logs while variables are not, and provides specific steps for handling and rotating credentials that have already been exposed in logs.

items.passage: # Responding to a suspected account compromise **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - Unrecognised activity appears in the audit log - A user reports credentials may have been exposed - Resources were created that nobody claims ## Common causes - Credentials were reused from a service that suffered a breach - An API key was committed to a public repository - A former team member retained access after leaving ## Resolution

items.title: Managing team members, roles and permissions
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Check the effective permissions view for the user, which resolves direct roles and group memberships together. 2. Confirm the invitation was accepted. Prefer group membership to direct role assignment, so that access can be reviewed in one place. ## Notes Removing the last account owner is not permitted. items.title: API key rotation and scope management

To rotate without downtime, create the replacement key first, deploy it, confirm traffic has moved, then revoke the old key. 4. If a key has been exposed publicly, revoke it immediately rather than waiting for the rotation window. ## Notes Keys issued to individual users are removed when that user is deleted. items.passage: # Handling exposed secrets and credential rotation **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - A key has been committed to a repository - A secret appears in application logs - A third party has reported finding a credential ## Common causes - Configuration was committed rather than referenced from the environment - The application prints its configuration during startup - A key was shared in a support ticket or a chat message ## Resolution

items.title: Connecting continuous integration pipelines
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Create a service account for the pipeline rather than using a personal key, so that access survives staff changes. 2. Grant the service account only the projects and permissions the pipeline needs, and review that grant when the pipeline changes. 3. Store the credential as an encrypted secret in your pipeline provider, never in the repository. 4. Test the pipeline credential separately from the deployment logic, so that authentication failures are distinguishable from deployment failures. ## Notes Service account keys do not expire by default. Set an expiry and rotate on a schedule.

Issue a replacement with the narrowest scope that still works, rather than recreating the original permissions by default. 3. Search the audit log for use of the exposed credential from unfamiliar addresses during the exposure window. 4. Add secret scanning to your pipeline so that the next occurrence is caught before it reaches a remote branch. ## Notes Never send a live credential to support. Support will never ask for one, and any credential shared in a ticket must be treated as exposed.
